assessment.headline: TSMC sees no AI demand slowdown, but CoreWeave debt stress and a $1T chip rout keep financing risk high.
assessment.digest_markdown:
## What changed this week

**Demand looks solid.** TSMC, the chipmaker that builds nearly every AI processor, beat its own forecast with Q3 revenue of $46.7B.

- It guided Q4 to $52.3-54.3B and kept 2026 capex at $60-64B.
- CEO C.C. Wei said he sees "no sign of slowdown."
- His one caution: rising component prices hurt consumer markets, so TSMC is planning 2027 prudently.
- Official Taiwan data agrees: AI-server suppliers' September revenue was up a median ~77% year on year.

**Money is the problem, not demand.** The week's sell-off was about financing and rates.

- Korea's KOSPI hit a circuit breaker.
- CNBC says twenty large AI and chip stocks lost more than $1T this week.
- CoreWeave, a heavily indebted GPU-cloud company, saw its 2031 bond yields top 15%, a distress-level reading.
- Nvidia's Jensen Huang said Nvidia sees no need to backstop CoreWeave.
- Oracle's credit-insurance (CDS) cost is quoted between ~151bp and a record 288bp. Neither figure comes from a major outlet.
- Junk-bond spreads widened 0.55 points in four weeks to 3.25%. Investment-grade spreads barely moved, so stress is still contained to riskier borrowers.

## Why it matters

The AI build-out is increasingly debt-funded. With the 10-year Treasury near 5.2% and oil above $120, weaker borrowers face higher costs. If financing dries up, capex could slow even while demand stays strong.

## What to watch

- Meta earnings on Oct 21, then Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon on Oct 28-29: capex guides and any "digestion" language.
- CoreWeave and Oracle credit pricing.
- Whether junk spreads keep widening.

*Not investment advice.*

amounts.sentence: As of June 30, 2026, we had additional leases, primarily for datacenters, that had not yet commenced of $ 329.1 billion, with some arrangements subject to certain contractual conditions being met.
As of June 30, 2026, we have entered into leases, primarily related to data centers, that have not yet commenced with future lease payments of $ 85.2 billion that are not yet recorded.

These lease obligations were approximately $278.99 billion, consisting of data centers, colocations, and certain network infrastructure, which will commence during the remainder of 2026 through 2036 with lease terms ranging from greater than one year to 30 years.
In July 2026, we entered into additional data center leases with lease obligations of approximately $68 billion, which are expected to commence in 2027 and 2028, with lease terms of 18 to 20 years.

As of August 31, 2026 , we had $ 288 billion of additional lease commitments, substantially all related to data center arrangements, that are generally expected to commence between the second quarter of fiscal 2027 a nd fiscal 2029 and for terms of fifteen to nineteen years that were not reflected on our condensed consolidated balance sheets as of August 31, 2026 or in the maturities table above.
